text.p: The following are the main stories from Tuesday morning's German newspapers:

- Leaders of the the current German government coalition insist they will stick together, with the main players urging each other to be more flexible on their differences, notably over the budget and ways to balance it.

- A constitutional court in North Rhine-Westphalia rejects complaints from six regional authorities against the Garzweiler II brown-coal production project, clearing the last effective legal hurdle against the plan.
- Germany's recession-hit construction industry will only see a pick-up in 1998, with a further 80,000 jobs expected to be lost this year, an employer body says.

- The government's new special deleguate for the eastern Germany states, Rudi Geil, encourages foreign firms to invest more in the region, noting that an investment promotion plan will soon be passed in parliament.
- Trade union leaders say they might be willing to consider clauses allowing construction firms in the east German industry to pay below collectively-agreed wage pacts in certain situations.

- Reports that the government was planning cuts in a number of welfare provisions, including measures designed to create jobs, draw criticism from a wide range of politicians, both within the government and outside, and trade unions.
- Germany grew as a site for the pharmaceutical industry with investments in the sector rising by nearly 12 percent in 1996 over the year before, according to an industry association.

- Senior executives of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) had an intensive three-hour meeting to discuss possible scenarios should the current coalition with the Free Democrats (FDP) founder. No way out of the current conflict with the FDP on how to balance the budget was however found.

- Fury is evident over Finance Minister Theo Waigel's comments that a new round of deep state spending cuts are required ahead of EMU, with opposition policiticians and trade unions focussing on the suggestion that existing aid to stimulate the jobs market could be cut.

- A mere one to two percent of some 4,000 top clergy in the east German Evangelical church worked in anyway for the Stasi, the state security service of the former Communist government there, a preliminary report by the Evangelical Church finds.

- Bavarian state politicians remain unconvinced by comments from Kohl that Europe's monetary union should and will go ahead on time, insisting that strict adherence to convergence criteria is more important than the timetable.
